clue.text: On which Kipling wrote sadly to mother an' dad; a poem followed

indicators.note: the words are treated sadly, knocked out of shape, so their letters must be rearranged
the next two words come after the rearranged section, building the title in sequence

blocks.note: taken as written, with the dropped letter of an' left out
taken as written
a lay is a short narrative poem or ballad

explanation.surface: Kipling, homesick and sorry for himself, pens a sad letter home to his parents, then adds a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: Kipling wrote on (about) the road to Mandalay, the title of his Burmese ballad, and a road is also something one could write on.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's famous poem from Barrack-Room Ballads is titled Mandalay and is known by its line about the road there.

clue.text: Suiting precious daughter

blocks.note: precious in the sense of affectedly dainty or quaint
D is the standard abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A doting parent picks out a fine outfit for a beloved daughter.
explanation.walkthrough: Suiting here is a noun, cloth for making suits, not the verb it appears to be.
explanation.definitionFit: Tweed is a rough woollen cloth traditionally made up into jackets and suits, so it is a kind of suiting material.

clue.text: Soak feet, say

blocks.note: first meaning: to overcharge or milk someone, take advantage of them
second meaning: feet as heard is feat, a daring deed

explanation.surface: Advice to soak one's tired feet, for instance in a basin of hot water.
explanation.walkthrough: Feet is not a definition as written: it is the sound-alike of feat, and a feat is an EXPLOIT. Soak means to fleece someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To exploit people is to take unfair advantage, as a landlord soaks tenants; as a noun an exploit is a bold deed or feat.

clue.text: Cetologist's quarry from Balearic Islands

indicators.note: from means only a part is taken out of the island names, with their opening letters left behind

blocks.note: Majorca and Minorca are two of the Balearic Islands, and both end in the same four letters

explanation.surface: A whale scientist hunts for specimens in the seas off the Spanish holiday islands.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural Islands is fair because ORCA can be taken from either Majorca (dropping MAJ) or Minorca (dropping MIN).
explanation.definitionFit: A cetologist studies whales and dolphins, and the orca or killer whale is one such marine mammal that could be studied.

clue.text: Tie up the Guardian's charge?

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is written from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: a ward is a person, usually a child, placed in the care of a legal guardian

explanation.surface: A question about tying up a payment owed to this newspaper, as if settling the Guardian's bill.
explanation.walkthrough: The Guardian looks like the newspaper and charge like a fee; here a guardian's charge is the person in their care.
explanation.definitionFit: A tie is a game or contest ending level, which is also called a draw.

clue.text: As was Ishmael or Socrates, I'd gathered

indicators.note: the letters are gathered up together and collected into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the comma and apostrophe

explanation.surface: A reader concludes that Ishmael, like Socrates, was shunned by his own society.
explanation.walkthrough: Ishmael in Genesis was cast out with his mother Hagar into the wilderness; Socrates seems to be a second example but is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ishmael was driven away from Abraham's household, and being banished or excluded from a community is being ostracised.

clue.text: Ordain, following Peter's habit

blocks.note: f. is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
Christ named Peter the rock on which he would build his church

explanation.surface: A new priest is ordained and dressed in the robes worn by St Peter.
explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions bracket the wordplay: to frock someone is to make them a priest, and a frock is a monk's habit.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, frock means invest with priestly office, the opposite of defrock; as a noun it is a monk's long gown or habit.

clue.text: Flower stemmers needed apres Louis XV and de Pompadour?

blocks.note: surface reading: gardeners or florists who strip stems from blooms

blocks.clueFragment: needed apres Louis XV and de Pompadour?
blocks.note: setter's reading: après nous le déluge, said by Madame de Pompadour to Louis XV, so a flower is something that flows and stemmers hold it back

explanation.surface: Florists are hired to trim the bouquets after a royal visit from Louis XV and his mistress.
explanation.walkthrough: A flower here is anything that flows, such as a river; things that stem a flow are sluices. The French quip promised a deluge after the king and his mistress were gone.
explanation.definitionFit: Sluice barriers on rivers and canals hold back or release water, stemming its flow, which is what floodgates do.

clue.text: Catastrophe liable to take issue with Polonius

indicators.note: the answer is taken straight out of the run of letters across the two neighbouring words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A disaster looms because someone is ready to quarrel with Polonius, the busybody of Hamlet.
explanation.walkthrough: Take issue looks like a phrase meaning argue; here issue means offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hamlet, Ophelia is the daughter of Polonius, so she is his issue, an old word for children or descendants.

clue.text: Packer down of dog

blocks.note: Kerry Packer was the Australian media tycoon who ran World Series Cricket
down and blue both mean low in spirits

explanation.surface: A furniture remover is feeling miserable about a dog.
explanation.walkthrough: Packer looks like someone who packs boxes; it is Kerry Packer, the Australian media magnate.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kerry blue is an Irish breed of terrier with a soft blue-grey coat, so it is a kind of dog.

clue.text: Might the next part come to one of the 25?

definitions.text: Might the next part come to one of the 25?

blocks.note: surface reading: a reader waiting for the next instalment of a story or serial
setter's reading: a lady in waiting, taken literally, is a pregnant woman awaiting the next generation, her baby

explanation.surface: A court attendant awaits the next episode of something being delivered to her.
explanation.walkthrough: The 25 are ladies in waiting; read literally, a lady in waiting is a woman expecting a baby, the next part of the family line.
explanation.definitionFit: A pregnant woman is waiting for her baby to come, so she is literally a lady waiting, a punning version of a court attendant.

clue.text: New look from this Christian

blocks.note: surface reading: a fresh appearance or a religious convert's change of outlook
setter's reading: the New Look was the 1947 fashion collection launched by a couturier whose first name was Christian

explanation.surface: A believer offers a fresh perspective on things.
explanation.walkthrough: Christian reads as a believer; it is the first name of the Paris couturier whose 1947 New Look collection changed post-war fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: Christian Dior was the French fashion designer, so his surname is what this Christian is called.

clue.text: See 1
Weak supporters touching caps once KKK den assembled

definitions.note: describes the legs rather than naming them

indicators.note: assembled means the letters are put together afresh, built into a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Feeble followers once tipped their hats at a gathering of the Ku Klux Klan.
explanation.walkthrough: Supporters are legs and the caps are kneecaps, which touch when the legs bow inwards; nothing here is about racist followers or doffed hats.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone knock-kneed has legs that bend inward so that the kneecaps touch, a weakness in their support.

clue.text: Who stole Shergar? Fish out one of the others!

indicators.note: out means the letters are put out of their order, scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written
the word as printed, but the parse needs an E where it has a second S: the setter's slip

explanation.surface: A question about the unsolved kidnapping of Shergar, then a call to haul in one of the gang responsible.
explanation.walkthrough: Shergar, the 1981 Derby winner, was stolen from an Irish stud in 1983 and never found. The likeliest reading is a jumble of FISH and OTHERS, but that has a second S where the answer needs a second E: a setter's slip.
explanation.definitionFit: Whoever took the racehorse Shergar committed the theft of a horse, so the culprit is by definition a horse thief.

clue.text: Film director resisting inclusion of tear-jerker

indicators.note: inclusion of means one word is placed inside the other

blocks.note: anti means against or opposed to
cutting an onion makes the eyes water

explanation.surface: A film director refuses to put a weepie into the schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: Tear-jerker suggests a sentimental film, which fits the director surface; here it is a vegetable that makes you cry.
explanation.definitionFit: Michelangelo Antonioni was the Italian film director of L'Avventura and Blow-Up.

clue.text: What Lindbergh used to ventilate WC?

blocks.note: to air a room is to ventilate it
W. C. Fields was the American comic actor

explanation.surface: A comic question about how the aviator freshened up the lavatory.
explanation.walkthrough: WC looks like a lavatory; it is the comedian W. C. Fields.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Lindbergh was a pioneering aviator, and pilots take off and land at aerodromes, the places his aircraft used.

clue.text: Show, in two senses, to have sickness benefit

indicators.note: the first piece is to have the second attached directly after it

blocks.note: an audio-visual show appeals to two senses, hearing and sight
an ail is an ailment or illness

explanation.surface: A government notice about how to claim sickness benefit.
explanation.walkthrough: AV is short for audio-visual, a presentation for eye and ear. Sickness benefit looks like one phrase but splits into wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Avail as a noun means use or advantage, as in to no avail, which is a benefit.

clue.text: Hydrophobic cab-driver madly spilling derv

indicators.note: the cab-driver spills fuel, losing those letters from the word
madly means the remaining letters run wild and settle in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, without the hyphen
derv is British slang for diesel fuel; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A taxi driver, terrified of water, frantically spills diesel all over the place.
explanation.walkthrough: Hydrophobia, fear of water, is a classic symptom of rabies, which is why it is used as an old name for the disease.
explanation.definitionFit: Rabic means relating to rabies, and hydrophobia was the old name for that disease, so hydrophobic is a synonym.

clue.text: Would Alfred tear into Beethoven''s first line in New York?

indicators.note: first asks for only the opening letter of the composer's name
into means the word goes inside the other letters

blocks.note: the initial letter of the composer's name
the El is New York's elevated railway line
to rend is to tear apart

explanation.surface: A question whether a pianist named Alfred would tear into Beethoven, perhaps on a train in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: Alfred Brendel was the Austrian pianist famed for his Beethoven, so the surface stays in his world. The definition gives only a first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Brendel, the Austrian-born concert pianist, is identified here by his first name alone.

clue.text: First new town wise about event, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the word is only a possible arrangement of letters, so they can be reordered
about means the first word is wrapped around the other

blocks.note: sage means wise
taken as written

explanation.surface: Planners show wisdom about some first event for a newly built town.
explanation.walkthrough: Stevenage in Hertfordshire was the first of Britain's post-war New Towns, designated in 1946.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevenage was the first town designated under the New Towns Act of 1946, built to rehouse Londoners.

clue.text: One said how he'd remain'd hopelessly in reserve

definitions.text: One said how he'd remain'd hopelessly in reserve

indicators.note: hopelessly means the letters are in a hopeless muddle, needing to be put in order

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone describes how a man was forced to stay, despairing, in a reservation.
explanation.walkthrough: How is the greeting given to Native Americans in old Westerns, and the reserve is a reservation; the whole clue describes the answer while also holding the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Amerind is a dated term for an American Indian, a people confined in the nineteenth century to reservations.

clue.text: Puck's pursuer on edge?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone chasing Puck, the mischievous sprite of A Midsummer Night's Dream
setter's reading: a hockey puck is chased by players on blades, which run on a sharp edge

explanation.surface: Someone chasing Shakespeare's mischievous fairy Puck is nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: On edge suggests anxiety; it is the steel edge of a blade on ice. Puck is the disc in ice hockey, not the fairy.
explanation.definitionFit: Ice hockey players chase the puck wearing blade boots, and they glide on the blade's edge.

clue.text: Newshound's epitaph?

blocks.note: surface reading: a journalist, someone who sniffs out stories
setter's reading: with 24, the words for a journalist's tombstone would be the reporter's time limit, read as a lifeless state plus a line of text

explanation.walkthrough: This light and 24 Down (See 21) together make DEADLINE: an epitaph is a line on a tomb about the dead, and a deadline is what governs a reporter's life.
explanation.definitionFit: Every journalist works to a fixed time for filing copy, and broken in two that word is a fitting inscription for a dead reporter.

clue.text: Samson destroyed his temple after many an attempt. Name?

blocks.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500, a large number
the indefinite article as a single letter
to have a go is to make an attempt
N is the standard abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: After many tries Samson finally pulled down a temple; whose was it?
explanation.walkthrough: In Judges, the blinded Samson pulled down the pillars of the temple of the Philistine god Dagon. Many as D (500) is a crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Dagon was the Philistine deity whose temple at Gaza collapsed when Samson pushed apart its pillars.

clue.text: With, for example, outside influence

indicators.note: outside means one word goes around the other, holding it within

blocks.note: say is used to introduce an example
W is short for with

explanation.surface: A phrase about having influence from outside, such as foreign pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold sway is to have power or influence over people, so the noun means control or influence.

clue.text: See 21

blocks.note: surface reading: a pointer to another clue, with nothing of its own
setter's reading: this light is the second half of the two-word phrase clued at 21 Across, a journalist's epitaph

explanation.walkthrough: The clue for this light is at 21 Across, Newshound's epitaph?, which answers in two halves: DEAD there and LINE here, making DEADLINE.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadline is the fixed time a reporter must file copy by; split, it reads as a line of text about the dead.

clue.text: One law is detaining unruly court attendants

indicators.note: unruly means the letters will not stay in line, so they are reordered

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A law is used to hold some troublemakers at court in custody.
explanation.walkthrough: Detaining looks like the container signal, but it is just part of the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Ladies-in-waiting are noblewomen who attend a queen or princess at the royal court.

clue.text: Sound, square and smelly

blocks.note: S is used as a short form of square, as in Sq. in addresses
olid is a rare word meaning foul-smelling

explanation.surface: Someone is described as healthy, conventional and in need of a bath.
explanation.walkthrough: OLID is a rare word for rank or fetid. Square giving a lone S is a loose abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Sound and solid both describe something firm, reliable and well founded, as in a sound or solid argument.

clue.text: Author with only a few (500) characters

indicators.note: characters means the letters of these words are used as raw material in another order

blocks.note: taken as written
D is the Roman numeral for 500

explanation.surface: A writer whose books have only a handful of characters, perhaps five hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: Characters suggests the people in a novel; it means letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Fay Weldon was the English novelist and screenwriter who wrote The Life and Loves of a She-Devil.
